title: Cold rebuild: which editor will Git open?
summary: Make nano the editor for Git and every other tool in a real shell, from memory, no hints.

steps.title: Cold rebuild
body: Time to prove a skill stuck. In *nano on servers* you made nano the editor for Git and every other tool, in a real shell.
Now do it again from memory: the same scenario, **no hints, no solution to peek at**. The checks are exactly the ones
Why: pulling something out of memory is what makes it stay there. If you get stuck, that is useful news: go back to
the lesson, then come back and try again tomorrow.
This check, plus the boss, is what proves the module.

steps.prompt: Why is nano often the right choice when you write instructions for a colleague on a production server?
options: What they type goes straight into the file and the exit keys are printed on screen, so a nervous typist cannot get stuck in a mode
It is faster than vim for every task
It is installed on every container image
steps.explain: nano is modeless and self-documenting. It is not everywhere (minimal images often have only `vi`, or nothing), which is why you learn vi too.

steps.title: Which editor will Git open? Cold
prompt: In `~/app`, Git and every other tool keep opening Vim.
1. Make Git use nano for every repository, with nothing in `~/app` overriding it.
2. Set `EDITOR` and `VISUAL` to nano for new shells, in `~/.bashrc`.
From memory: no hints this time. Prove it with the command that prints the editor Git would run.
